opener.caption: Each group of this chapter opens with the question a reader brings, and its forms answer it.

intro: This chapter sets how Oath & Action shows numbers. Fourteen rules come first and hold for every chart. Each form a chart can take then has its own entry, grouped by the question it answers, with when to use it, what to use instead, and a finished example that our chart kit draws from frozen data, with its table as live text.

Chapter 13 sets the evidence every chart carries: its label, its grade, its source line and its dates. The rules here cite those rules by number and add what a drawing needs, from its scale and colors to its labels, its phone drawing and its files.

groups.title: Every chart
groups.line: Fourteen rules hold for every chart, from the question it answers to the files it ships as.

groups.title: Comparison: which is bigger, and how do they rank?
groups.line: Bars, dots and slopes set values side by side on one scale, so a reader sees which is bigger and by how much.

groups.title: Shift and swing: what moved, and which way?
groups.line: Arrows, lollipops and diverging bars show which way each value moved and how far, with the direction in a word as well as a mark.

groups.title: Change over time: how has it moved?
groups.line: Time runs from left to right in lines, columns and timelines, with each gap, break and preliminary value marked where it falls.

groups.title: Composition: what is it made of?
groups.line: Stacked bars, unit charts and treemaps show the parts of a whole and print the whole they add up to.

groups.title: Distribution and density: how are the values spread?
groups.line: Histograms, strip plots and box plots show how values spread, where they bunch and how far they run.

groups.title: Correlation: do two things move together?
groups.line: Scatter plots and their relatives show whether two measures move together, and an association’s note says what the pattern cannot show about cause.

groups.title: Uncertainty and estimates: how sure is it?
groups.line: A range, a band or a fan shows how sure a figure is, as its publisher states it, and an estimate’s note gives the method behind its range (Rule 13.1).

groups.title: Gauges and indicators: where does it stand now?
groups.line: Big numbers give a figure with the context to judge it, and progress bars and bullet graphs set one measure against its target or limit. Step trackers and status chips show how far a bill or a dispute has come.

groups.title: Tables and plain words: where does a reader look things up, and when do words answer faster?
groups.line: A table lets a reader look a value up, and one sentence answers when a single figure is the whole story.

rules.title: Start from the reader’s question, then choose the form.
rule: Write down the question a reader brings to the numbers, in the words a reader would use, before choosing a form. The question names the comparison: which is bigger, what moved, how it changed, what it is made of, where it happens, or how sure a figure is. Each group of this chapter opens with one of those questions, and each entry in the group says when its form fits the data at hand.
When one figure answers the question, a sentence carries it (Rule 14.134). When a reader needs to look values up, a table does (Rule 14.133).

text: Each form answers one kind of question well. Bars sorted by size show which year was largest and hide the order of the years, so a reader who asked how something changed cannot see the change.

rules.builders: Write reader_question in the spec first, then pick the form from the group whose question matches; the kit draws it with node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build <spec>.

specs.label: First step
specs.value: The reader’s question, in a reader’s words, written into the chart’s spec before any drawing

specs.label: Question to form
specs.value: The question that opens each group of this chapter, then the entry whose use names the data at hand

specs.label: One figure
specs.value: A sentence, Rule 14.134

specs.label: Values to look up
specs.value: A table, Rule 14.133

correct.caption: The question asks how applications changed, so the years run left to right on one line, and the jump after 2019 shows at once: from 3.5 million to 5.4 million in two years.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.1. The reader asked how applications changed, and bars sorted by size put 2025 first and 2009 last, so the years fall out of order and the jump after 2019 cannot be seen.

rules.title: Build every chart in one anatomy, from evidence label to table.
rule: Every chart prints the same eight parts in the same order, so a reader always knows where to look: the evidence label and grade line (Rules 13.1 and 13.2), the title, the measure line (Rule 13.7), the reading guide, the chart, its notes, the source line (Rule 13.6) and the table (Rule 14.13).

The title is one full sentence, and house rule H08 sizes its claim. A chart of dollars across years says in its measure line “not adjusted for inflation”, or names the dollars’ year and the price index that adjusted them. The reading guide says in a sentence or two how to read the drawing. Notes carry what the drawing cannot. A part with nothing to say is left out, and the rest keep their order.

text: Readers learn where things are after a few charts. When every chart puts its source in the same place, a reader can check any figure in seconds, and a chart that lacks a part shows the gap.

rules.builders: Fill every word field of the spec, as the kit’s README sets out under “The keys a spec takes”; the kit prints the parts in this order and leaves out an empty one.

specs.label: Order
specs.value: Evidence label and grade line, title, measure line, reading guide, chart, notes, source line, table

specs.label: Evidence label
specs.value: On the chip fill, in the label style

specs.label: Grade line for a count of the atlas’s records
specs.value: “Graded by the atlas, claim by claim: our count of its register of claims”, or record by record for its issue records, since the atlas grades each record and never the count (Rule 13.1)

correct.caption: The eight parts in order, each numbered where the kit prints it. The table sits folded under the source line.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.2. The title names a topic and states no finding, and the chart drops its label, measure line, notes and source line, so a reader cannot tell what was counted or who counted it.

rules.title: Label the data directly, and use a key only when labels cannot fit.
rule: Rule 12.6 sets where a label sits. In a chart, each line takes its name beside it toward its last point, where the lines stand apart, each bar its value at its end, and each group its name on or beside its marks, in the text’s ink. Units go once in the measure line, so a label carries its number with at most a sign or a percent sign.

A key earns its place only when a mark codes something a label cannot carry on every mark, such as an evidence grade, a pattern or a run of shades. Then it sits under the measure line, in the order the marks run, as Rule 12.6 sets.

text: A reader matching inks between a key and the lines looks away from the data at every step, and close inks are hard to match at all in grayscale or with a color vision deficiency. A name beside each line is read in place.

rules.builders: Name each series in the spec’s labels.series; the kit sets the names at the line ends and warns when one cannot fit.

specs.label: A line
specs.value: Its name beside it, toward its last point, in the label ink

specs.label: A bar
specs.value: Its value at its end, its name beside it

specs.label: Units
specs.value: Once, in the measure line

specs.label: A key
specs.value: Only for a code no label can carry, under the measure line, in the order the marks run (Rule 12.6)

correct.caption: Each line carries its own name beside it, so a reader reads the age group in place, and the youngest group, which the title names, takes the view’s red.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.3. Four lines in four inks send the reader down to a key and back for every line, where a name beside each line would be read in place.

rules.title: Start bars and columns at zero, keep one scale per axis, and size circles by area.
rule: Draw an amount at its true size. Bars and columns start at zero, because a reader compares their lengths. A line may start above zero when the change is the point, with the axis labeled where it starts.

Each axis keeps one scale, so two measures take two panels side by side rather than a second axis on the right. A circle that stands for an amount takes its area from the value, so its radius grows with the square root of the value.

text: Readers judge a bar by its length before they read its number. Cut the axis at 55 percent and 1992’s 67.7 percent stands 3.7 times as tall as 1996’s 58.4, for a gap of 9.3 points.

rules.builders: The kit draws every bar and column from zero and fails a circle not sized by area; scale may set a line’s range, never a bar’s.

specs.label: Bars and columns
specs.value: From a zero line drawn at the baseline weight

specs.label: A line
specs.value: May start above zero, with the axis labeled at its start

specs.label: Two measures
specs.value: Two panels on two scales, side by side

specs.label: Circles
specs.value: Area in proportion to the value, so the radius follows its square root

correct.caption: From zero, each column keeps its true size: the highest share, 67.7 percent in 1992, stands about 16 percent taller than the lowest, 58.4 percent in 1996.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.4. The axis starts at 55 percent, so 1992’s column stands 3.7 times as tall as 1996’s for a gap of 9.3 points.

rules.title: Give each color in a chart one job from the four data palettes.
rule: Each palette does one job, and a chart uses one palette for each thing its colors encode. Sequential Verdigris runs one measure from low to high. Diverging pair B runs above and below a midpoint, as Rule 01.3 sets. The four group inks name up to four groups, always in the order Charcoal, Verdigris, Prussian, then Stone, which carries its hatch. The Stone magnitude steps show size with no direction.
Steps of one hue promise an order, so named groups take the group inks and a measure takes a scale. Rule 05.7 sets the subject, the context and the one red point inside any of them.

text: A reader takes a color’s meaning from the first chart and carries it to the next. When each palette keeps its one job across our work, a reader who has learned that a stronger green means more can trust it on every page.

rules.builders: Name a color role in the form (seq-1 to seq-5, div-1 to div-5, cat-1 to cat-4, mag-1 to mag-4); a spec never names a color.

specs.label: Sequential
specs.value: Five steps of Verdigris, light to dark for low to high

specs.label: Diverging, pair B
specs.value: Five steps, Prussian through the page color to Verdigris (Rule 01.3)

specs.label: Groups
specs.value: Charcoal, Verdigris, Prussian, Stone with its hatch, in that order; four at most (Rule 14.8)

specs.label: Magnitude
specs.value: Four steps of Stone

correct.caption: The four palettes, each beside its one job and the question it answers. The fourth group ink always carries its hatch, so it reads apart from the third in grayscale.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.5. Four ways to reach the county take four steps of one green, so the key reads as a scale from less to more, though the channels have no order.

rules.title: Spend the view’s one red on the point the title names.
rule: Rule 05.3 gives each view one working red and says which job claims it first. In a chart, the red goes to the one point, bar or line the title names, inside the 1 px Charcoal keyline of Rule 05.5, and that mark carries its own label. Marks the title names together, such as the bars of one age band, share the red. Every other mark takes the light fill on Newsprint and the context ink on Charcoal (Rule 05.7).

A line or a single bar is one mark, and a run of columns is a set of marks, so a title can name one column of a run and give it the red, as on Rule 14.12’s plate. A chart that draws only one line, bar or path has no other mark to set it apart from, so the mark takes Charcoal at the subject weight and the value the title names carries a label. When the title names a second mark only to measure the first against, as “more than twice Zion’s” does on this rule’s plate, that mark is a comparison. It keeps the light fill with its label, and the red stays on the finding.

The named mark gives up the red and takes Charcoal at the subject weight, with its label, in two cases: when an error or a step the reader can take already holds the view’s red, and when a reader would tie the mark to a party. A state, a Congress or chamber whose majority readers know, an election result, money spent to elect a candidate and a policy readers link to one party all carry that tie, and red on them reads as a party’s color (Rules 01.1, 01.2 and 14.7).

A title that states two findings, each on its own, such as the most and the least, sets both marks in Charcoal the same way, since two reds would split the reader’s first look. Rule 05.1 keeps the red within 5 percent of the drawing at every width, so a named mark that would pass that share, such as a part of a treemap, pie or donut, or a tall column in a short run, takes Charcoal at the subject weight as well. Red never codes a series, a group, a step on a scale or a sign, such as a deficit or a loss.

text: One red mark tells a reader where to look first, and the title tells them why. A second red mark splits their attention, and red that codes a group reads as a warning about that group.

rules.builders: Name the one point in the spec’s labels.point, which draws it in red with its keyline and every other mark in the light fill; where the subject ink takes its place, labels.named does it instead, with a list for two marks. The kit counts working reds and fails a view whose red falls on two jobs or covers more than 5 percent of the drawing at any width it checks.

correct.caption: The title names Great Smoky Mountains, and its bar alone takes the view’s red, inside its keyline. Zion, which the title names only to compare, stays gray with its value like every other park.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.6. Red falls on three parks while the title names one, so a reader cannot tell which bar the title means.

rules.title: Tell parties apart by name, place and shape, with no red and blue.
rule: Rule 01.2 draws every party in one neutral ink with its name on the mark, and Rule 01.1 keeps red off every party. A chart then tells parties apart by what a reader can read without color: the name on or beside each mark, the mark’s place in the order, a solid and an open mark where two sides sit side by side, and a word or sign for direction, as in “Republican +2.2”.
No election graphic pairs red with blue, social cards included, and Prussian never stands for a party.

text: Red and blue turn a chart of results into team colors, and a reader decides which side the chart is on before reading a number. A name on each mark gives readers on both sides the same facts, in color or in grayscale.

rules.builders: Party data takes the party role in any form; the kit fails a party mark in Pillar Red or Prussian.

specs.label: Party marks
specs.value: One neutral ink for every party, Charcoal on Newsprint

specs.label: Two sides at a glance
specs.value: One solid and one open mark, in the same ink (Rule 01.2)

specs.label: Direction
specs.value: An arrow, the mark’s place or a printed lead, such as “Republican +2.2”

specs.label: Never
specs.value: Red against blue, or Prussian for a party

correct.caption: Every party takes the same ink and its name, so the bars compare seats and nothing else.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.7. Red and blue stand for the parties and a key holds their initials, so the chart reads as one team against another and loses the parties in grayscale.

rules.title: Past four groups, split into small multiples or set one group in ink against gray.
rule: The four group inks of Rule 14.5 are as many as a reader can tell apart and hold in mind. With five or more groups, draw one small panel for each on a shared scale, or draw the group the title names in ink and the others in gray. Either way, every group carries its name on the chart.
Rule 14.23 shows small multiples of bars, Rule 14.30 small multiples of lines, and Rule 14.31 one line in ink over a field of gray.

text: Past four, the inks start to look alike and the key grows longer than a reader will hold. Small panels on one scale let a reader take each group’s shape and level one at a time, and still compare them.

rules.builders: Use multi-line-highlight or small-multiple-bars for five or more groups; the kit fails a key of more than four inks.

specs.label: Groups in color
specs.value: Four at most, in Rule 14.5’s order

specs.label: Five or more
specs.value: Small multiples on one shared scale, or one group in ink and the rest in gray

specs.label: Names
specs.value: Every group named on the chart, in its panel or beside its line

correct.caption: Each panel sets one age group in ink against the other four in gray, on one scale, so a reader compares five groups without a key.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.8. Five groups take five inks, the fifth borrowed from a scale, and the key under the plot asks the reader to match each one.

rules.title: Show the publisher’s uncertainty, and rank only where a gap passes the margin of error.
rule: Rule 13.5 draws a survey figure’s margin of error as an interval. A chart that ranks survey figures, or singles one out as higher or lower than another, does so only where the gap between them passes the gap’s own margin of error at the publisher’s stated confidence, and a note says so. Figures whose gaps sit inside it are drawn and described as alike: an open dot, a shared place, or the words “within the margin of error”.
A count of every case, such as votes cast or seats held, has no sampling margin and ranks as it stands.

text: A survey measures a sample, so each figure could sit anywhere in its interval. Two states three points apart, each with a margin near three points, may stand in either order across the whole population, and a ranking that puts one first tells a reader something the survey cannot know.

rules.builders: Take the margin the publisher prints for the figure drawn, and compute one only where it prints none, saying so in the sidecar. Carry each figure’s margin in its own column of the data; a form draws the interval from it and the note names the confidence.

specs.label: Interval
specs.value: The publisher’s margin of error at its stated confidence, a line through the dot

specs.label: A gap’s margin, two separate places
specs.value: The square root of the sum of their squared margins

specs.label: A gap’s margin, a place inside an area
specs.value: The square root of the sum of the two squared margins less twice the place’s squared margin times its share of the units the area’s figure counts, such as people or households; where the data hold no share, the first test, and the note says it treats the two as independent

specs.label: Within the margin
specs.value: An open dot and the words “within the margin of error”

specs.label: Counts
specs.value: No sampling margin; they rank as they stand

correct.caption: Each state’s line shows its margin of error. Five states sit past the margin from the nation and take a filled dot; the five within it take an open one, and the chart ranks none of them.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.9. The ranks put Michigan first and Texas last, but Michigan’s lead over Pennsylvania, 2.6 points, and Texas’s gap below New York, 1.3 points, both sit inside the margin of error, so the survey cannot order them.

rules.title: Choose the window from the question, and draw an inauguration only as a dated note.
rule: Choose the window, the first and last period a chart shows, from the reader’s question, and print its reason in the measure line: the first year a series exists, the first year a method holds, the span the question names, or a round span back from the latest figure when no earlier start has a reason of its own. Rule 13.7 gives charts shown together one window.

An inauguration or an election may appear inside the window as a dated note on an unbroken line. The line keeps one ink and one weight across the date, and no band, color or break divides the period into one officeholder’s years and another’s (house rule H09).

text: A window that starts where a line looks best can make a long fall look like a rise, and a reader cannot see what was left out. Bands at each inauguration ask the reader to credit or blame each officeholder for whatever the line does inside them, which the chart cannot show.

rules.builders: Put the window’s reason in measure_line and any event in annotations; the kit draws one line with no band.

specs.label: Window
specs.value: From the question, its reason printed in the measure line

specs.label: Charts shown together
specs.value: One window, printed once (Rule 13.7)

specs.label: An event
specs.value: A dated note with a leader, on an unbroken line

specs.label: An inauguration
specs.value: No band, color change or break at the date (house rule H09)

correct.caption: The window runs from the first year these industry codes allow to the latest count, and the measure line says so. The line runs unbroken across every inauguration in it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.10. Bands at each inauguration cut a 25-year fall into four presidencies, so the drawing invites a reader to credit or blame each president for a decline that runs through all four terms.

rules.title: Mark a gap, a break in a series or a preliminary value in the drawing.
rule: Draw what the data lacks or changes where it happens. A month or year with no figure leaves a gap in the line, and the line never bridges it. Where a publisher changes its method, the line breaks, the year prints both estimates, and a note says what changed. A preliminary value takes an open mark and the word preliminary beside it, and the qualification names it (Rule 13.7).

text: A line drawn through a missing month invents a value, and a line run across a change of method shows the change as a jump in what was measured. Marking each one where it falls lets a reader see what the data can and cannot say.

rules.builders: Mark breaks in the data’s break column and preliminary rows in its status column; the kit leaves the gap and opens the mark.

specs.label: No figure
specs.value: A gap in the line, with a note that says why

specs.label: A change of method
specs.value: A break, both estimates printed, a note that names the change

specs.label: Preliminary
specs.value: An open mark and the word preliminary; the qualification names it (Rule 13.7)

correct.caption: The line breaks in 2013 and draws both of that year’s estimates, so a change of method never reads as a change in income; the table gives both estimates for 2013 and for 2017.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.11. One line runs through both of 2013’s estimates and both of 2017’s, so a change in the survey’s questions draws as a jump in income.

rules.title: Redraw for a phone only when the form must change, and keep the data and finding.
rule: Draw a chart once for every width when its form still reads at 358 px. Change the form for a phone only when it must: when labels would fall under 13 px (Rule 06.3), when columns grow too narrow to carry their values, or when arrows grow too short to read. Columns then become bars, and a map of arrows becomes a list.
The phone drawing keeps every row, the title, the finding and the source line, and a note under the drawing carries any words that leave the plot.

text: Many readers meet our charts on a phone first. A drawing redrawn for no reason gives them a second picture to learn, and one that drops rows or changes its title gives phone readers a different finding from everyone else.

rules.builders: Set phone to differs and write phone_note in the spec when the form changes; the kit draws both and checks each at 358 px.

specs.value: When every label and mark reads at that width

specs.value: Columns as bars, arrows as a list, when the first form cannot carry its words

specs.value: Every row, the title, the finding and the source line

correct.caption: At full width the twelve years stand as columns, each value above its column. On a phone the values would not fit, so the columns become bars, with the same rows, title and finding.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.12. The phone drawing keeps three of the twelve years and takes a new title, so a reader on a phone meets a different finding from a reader at a desk.

rules.title: Carry every chart’s table as live text, and publish the still image first.
rule: Every chart carries its table: the rows it draws, as live text that a screen reader, a search and a copy can reach, folded under the source line as “The table and notes”. Rule 18.10 sets the table’s markup. With scripts off, the table stands open and the chart’s description takes the drawing’s place.

Design the still image first, for a newsletter, an email or a social card, where nothing moves and nothing answers a pointer. A value a reader needs prints on the chart or in its notes. An interactive layer on the website adds filters or a switch to the still chart and takes nothing away from it.

text: Many readers meet a chart as a still picture in an inbox, where hovering does nothing. A table in live text gives every reader the numbers, whether they listen to the page, search it or copy a figure into their own notes.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2, success criterion 1.1.1, Non-text Content, and design judgment, from the chart system our founder and editor approved in November 2026

rules.builders: Fill the spec’s table, as the kit’s README sets out under “The keys a spec takes”; the kit writes the table, and its check fails one whose rows differ from the data.

specs.value: The table open and the description in the drawing’s place

specs.value: Designed first; every value a reader needs printed

specs.value: Adds to the still chart on the website, and drops nothing from it

correct.caption: Each column prints its value, so the still image needs no pointer, and the table under the source line gives the same rows as live text.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.13. The values show only in a tooltip, which a newsletter, an email and a screen reader never reach, and the chart carries no table.

rules.title: Export every chart from the kit, so its files match the page.
rule: Make every file of a chart with the chart kit’s one command, from the same spec and data file the page draws. The kit writes three files for each ground and width: an SVG with the chart’s title and description inside it, a PNG at twice size, and a CSV of exactly the rows the chart draws. Each name carries the date, what the chart is, its ground and its width, as Rule 18.14 asks of a download.

text: A file made by hand drifts from the page the first time someone fixes one and forgets the other. One command from one spec keeps the drawing, the still image and the numbers in step, and the kit checks the CSV against the table each time it runs.

rules.builders: Run node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build <spec> --out <folder>; never edit an exported file, edit the spec and run it again.

specs.label: Files
specs.value: SVG, PNG at twice size, CSV of the drawn rows

specs.label: Names

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.14. Each file was made by hand: the screenshot drops the source line, the retyped numbers round away the table’s values, and the redrawn picture no longer matches the page.

rules.title: Rank bars from the longest when the order is the answer.
rule: Draw one bar per category from a zero line, longest first unless the categories keep an order of their own, with the full name at the left and the total at the bar’s end. A bar may split into parts that stay apart in gray print by fill, outline, hatch and dash, named in a key above the bars.

text: Readers judge length from a shared zero line more exactly than any other mark, and sorting puts the answer at the top of the chart. A bar laid on its side leaves room for a category’s full name, so nobody has to decode an abbreviation.

rules.builders: Form ranked-bar: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s03, or copy specs/s03.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.parts names each part and its style.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which category is biggest and by how much, among a dozen or fewer whose names are too long to sit under columns.

use_instead.when: A few categories or a short run of years reads best from left to right
Dozens of items sit on one scale, or their values sit far from zero
A long ranked list would form one dark block of bars
The parts of each bar add to one whole and their shares are the point

correct.caption: Who changed the rules: voters, courts or legislatures?

rules.title: Use columns for a few categories or a short run of years.
rule: Use columns to compare a few counts side by side, or one count over a short run of years read from left to right, such as the laws each Congress enacted. Start every column at zero (Rule 14.4), and print each value at the column’s end and its name below it. The column the title names takes the red point, or the text’s ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, and the rest take light gray.
When a phone leaves too little room to print every name and value, the columns turn into bars read from top to bottom in the same order (Rule 14.12).

text: Every column stands on the same zero line, so the eye compares heights as amounts. Readers take left to right as the order of time, which suits a count per year or per term. Past a dozen or so, columns thin into a fence the eye cannot sort, and a line shows the same run more clearly.

rules.builders: Form column: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s17, or copy specs/s17.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.point draws the column the title names in red with the rest in light gray, and labels.named sets it in the text’s ink instead (Rule 14.6).
rules.use_when: The reader asks how a handful of counts compare, or how one count changed across a few years or terms of office, and each value matters on its own.

use_instead.when: The categories have long names, there are more than about a dozen, or they read best ranked by size
The run of years is long and the shape of the change matters more than any one value
Monthly values swing so much that the trend needs an average drawn through them
Each category carries two or three measures that the reader compares within it
The values run above and below zero and their direction is the point

correct.caption: How many bills became law in each Congress?

rules.title: Add a benchmark tick when each bar has a fair share to meet.
rule: Draw one bar per group from zero and cross it with a short tick at the value the reader should compare it with, such as the 20 percent of households each fifth holds. Print the bar’s value at its end, name the tick once above the first bar, and draw the tick in ink with an edge of the ground’s color so it shows across the bar.

text: A share means little until the reader knows what share to expect. The tick puts that expectation on every bar, so the gap shows as distance on the same scale and nobody has to subtract one number from another.

rules.builders: Form bar-benchmark-tick: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s18, or copy specs/s18.json and point it at a new dataset; encode.benchmark names the column the tick draws.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how a group’s share compares with its size, or how each result compares with a target or a national figure.

use_instead.when: Each row compares two times or two measures, with no fixed value to meet
The reader needs only the order of the groups, with nothing to compare each one against
One value moves toward a target through ranges marked poor, fair and good
The parts add to one whole and the reader asks how the whole divides

correct.caption: What share of all household income goes to each fifth of households?

rules.title: Use a dot plot to set many items on one scale.
rule: Give each item one row: its name at the left, a dot at its value and the value printed in a column at the right edge, sorted so the order answers the reader’s question. Draw a figure the reader compares against, such as all states together, as a labeled line across the rows, and mark rows counted another way with an open dot and a key.

text: A dot marks a position without the weight of a bar, so 50 rows stay light enough to scan and the eye follows the line of dots down the ranking. The printed column lets a reader find an exact figure without reading it off the scale.

rules.builders: Form dot-plot: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s19, or copy specs/s19.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.reference names the row drawn as the line, labels.open the status drawn as an open dot.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where one item stands among dozens, such as their own state among 50, and the values sit far from zero or close together.

use_instead.when: There are a dozen items or fewer and their size from zero is the point
Each item has two values, such as two years, and the change between them matters
Each value is a survey estimate whose margin of error decides the order
The reader asks how the values spread, and no single item matters

correct.caption: How many residents per 100,000 does each state hold in prison?

rules.title: Use a dumbbell for two values in each row and the gap between.
rule: Join each row’s two values with a line on one scale for every row, the earlier as an open dot and the later filled, and print both values beside their dots. When the scale starts above zero, say where in the measure line, and test each change against its margin of error before the words call it a change (Rule 14.9).

text: The line between the dots draws the gap itself, so a reader sees its size without subtracting, and the two dot styles keep the years apart in gray print. A dot carries no length from zero, so the scale may start where the data starts, as long as the chart says so.

rules.builders: Form dumbbell: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s04, or copy specs/s04.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.from and labels.to name the two series values.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how far apart two values are for each group, such as the same age group in two elections, and which way each one moved.

use_instead.when: About ten items or fewer at two points in time, where a change in their order matters
The rows differ so much in size that a small row’s two dots would sit on top of each other, so each row’s change reads better as a percent
The direction and size of each shift matter more than the two values
The reader compares two to four measures per category as lengths from zero

correct.caption: Which age groups report voting, and did that change between two elections?

rules.title: Use a slope chart to compare about ten items at two points in time.
rule: Draw each item as a straight line from its earlier value on the left axis to its later value on the right, printing the earlier value at the left and the later value with the item’s name at the right. Give the item the title names the red point, or the text’s ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, with the rest in light gray, and print both years over the axes.
Choose the two years for a reason the measure line states, and when a longer record would change how a reader sees the move, give that record in a note (Rule 14.10).

text: The angle of each line shows the direction and size of a change at a glance, and lines that cross show a change in order that two lists of numbers hide. Two points alone say nothing about the years between them, so the chart owes the reader the reason for its dates.

rules.builders: Form slope: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s20, or copy specs/s20.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.from and labels.to name the two times, and labels.point the item in red.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which items rose and which fell between two dates, and how their order changed.

use_instead.when: The years between the two points matter, or there are more than two
More than about ten items, whose lines would cross into a tangle, so each needs a row of its own
The reader asks how far each item moved and toward which side

correct.caption: Did younger households lose ground on owning a home?

rules.title: Use lollipops when a long ranked list would look heavy as bars.
rule: Draw each row as a thin stem from the zero line to a dot at its value, print the value past the dot and the name at the left, and sort the rows so the order answers the question. Give the row the title names the red point, or the text’s ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, with the rest in light gray.

text: A stem keeps the length a reader compares from the zero line while putting little ink on the page, so a long list stays easy to scan. The dot marks where each length ends, which is the one place the eye needs.

rules.builders: Form lollipop: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s21, or copy specs/s21.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.point names the row in red, and labels.named lists rows set in the text’s ink.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which items lead a ranking of a dozen or more, and the values sit close enough that solid bars would form one dark block.

use_instead.when: There are a dozen rows or fewer, or each bar splits into parts
The values sit far from zero, so the reader compares positions along one scale
Each row carries a change from one value to another

correct.caption: Which everyday answers rest on the most claims?

rules.title: Use grouped bars when two to four measures share each category.
rule: Set the series side by side within each category, in the four-ink order with the fourth hatched (Rule 14.5), start every bar at zero and print each value at its end. Name each series after its value in the first group, so the chart needs no key (Rule 14.3).

Past four series, split into small multiples (Rule 14.8). When the title names a gap between two survey estimates, test it against the margin of error first and say in a note that it passes (Rule 14.9).

text: A reader compares bars that touch first, so grouping decides which comparison the reader makes. Grouping by category puts the two series of each category side by side, which suits a gap within each group, and the eye can still run down one series’ bars to compare across groups.

rules.builders: Form grouped-bar: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s22, or copy specs/s22.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.series sets each series’ name and the order its bars draw.
rules.use_when: The reader compares two to four series within each category first, such as men and women at each age, and across categories second.

use_instead.when: There are more than four series, or the reader compares one series across categories and the others only distract
The series are two dates for the same item and the change is the point
The series are parts that add to one whole

correct.caption: How does taking part in the labor force differ by age for men and women?

rules.title: Repeat one small bar chart per group when groups need comparing.
rule: Draw the same bars in one panel per group, on one scale shared by every panel, with the categories in the same order in each, so the eye compares a bar with the bar in the same place next door. Give each panel a title with its group and its size, and place as many panels across as fit, one across on a phone. The one bar the title names takes the red point, or the text’s ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, and every other bar takes light gray.

text: Panels that repeat one design let the reader learn the chart once and then read every group the same way. A shared scale keeps a long bar in one panel the same size as a long bar in another, which separate scales would break without any sign on the page.

rules.builders: Form small-multiple-bars: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s23, or copy specs/s23.json and point it at a new dataset; encode.panel names the column that splits the panels, labels.point the one bar in red by panel and category, and scale.x the scale they share, from zero to the largest value when it is left out.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how the same mix or ranking differs from group to group, such as the evidence grades behind each topic, or there are more groups than four inks can carry (Rule 14.8).

use_instead.when: There are two to four groups and the reader compares them within each category
Each group’s parts add to one whole and the whole is the point
Each group is one value, so a panel would hold one bar

correct.caption: How sure is the evidence behind each of the five topic hubs?

rules.title: Avoid radar charts, whose shapes change with the order of their spokes.
rule: Leave radar charts out of every Oath & Action piece. Draw the same measures as grouped bars from one zero line, a dot plot on one scale, or small-multiple bars with one panel per group, so each value is read as a length from zero or a position.

text: A radar chart draws values as a shape, and a shape’s area grows with the square of its values, so a group a little ahead on every spoke looks far bigger. Moving one spoke to another place changes every shape on the chart with no change in the data, and overlapping outlines hide each other.

rules.builders: No form: the kit draws no radar chart. The sketch, work/build/guide/specimens/s-14-24-sketch.html, draws the radar twice with its spokes in two orders beside grouped bars of the same values; build the better choice with the grouped-bar, dot-plot or small-multiple-bars form.
rules.sketch_alt: Two radar charts draw the same illustrative values for two groups with their spokes in different orders, and the dark group’s shape is the larger in the first and the smaller in the second. Beside them, grouped bars of the same values show the dark group ahead on two measures and behind on three.
rules.use_when: Never: a reader who asks how several groups compare across the same measures gets a truer answer from grouped bars, a dot plot or small-multiple bars.

use_instead.when: Each group has one value on each of several measures and the reader compares positions
The reader compares each group’s mix of measures, panel by panel
The reader compares two to four groups within each measure

correct.caption: Two radar charts draw the same illustrative values for two groups with their spokes in different orders, and the dark group’s shape is the larger in the first and the smaller in the second.
correct.label: Radar chart, a form that misleads

rules.title: Draw each item’s move between two dates as an arrow from start to end.
rule: Use shift arrows when the reader needs where each item started, where it ended and which way it moved. Give each item one row, with an arrow from the earlier value to the later one on one scale with a labeled center, and set the national row apart above the states (Rule 14.7 for party data). On a phone, where the arrows crowd, the chart ranks the items by the size of the shift and draws each as a stem from zero, with the later value in words on its row.

text: An arrow carries three facts at once: the start, the end and the direction, so a reader sees both that every state moved one way and how far apart they still stand. Party names in words and position carry the sides (Rule 14.7).

rules.builders: Form shift-arrows: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s11; encode from, to and shift, and the form draws the phone ranking under 480 px.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which places moved, which way and how far, between two elections or two years.

use_instead.when: Only the size of each move matters, ranked
The places should be read as a map of the country
The reader looks up each place’s figures more than the shape of the moves

correct.caption: Which states moved toward which party between 2020 and 2024, and how far?

rules.title: Rank one change per item as a stem from zero, longest first.
rule: Use a change lollipop when each item has one change between two dates. Draw a stem from zero to the change with a dot at its end, rank the items from the largest change, print each change beside its dot, and set the national figure apart at the top. Set the names flush left at the drawing’s edge, and label a gridline at a round change, such as +100 for a doubling, so the reader can judge a stem’s length. Position and the printed sign carry the direction.

text: Ranking by the size of the change answers the reader’s question in the order they ask it. A stem from zero gives each change a length the eye can compare, as a bar does (Rule 14.4), and the key ties that length to a number. The dot marks where each change stops with less ink than a full bar, so 50 rows stay light.

rules.builders: Form change-lollipop: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s24; give it two rows per item with labels.from and labels.to, or one change column as encode.value.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which places or groups moved most between two dates, and the size of each move matters more than where each one started.

use_instead.when: Where each item started and ended matters as much as how far it moved
Some items gained and others lost, and the reader needs both sides of a baseline
Both values for each item matter, and the change is one of several readings

correct.caption: Where did applications to start a business rise most since 2019?

rules.title: Draw gains and losses as bars from one zero line, losses to the left.
rule: Use a diverging bar when items moved both ways from a baseline: start every bar on one zero line, send losses left and gains right, order the bars by size, and print each figure with its sign. Pair B’s two end steps may repeat the direction in color, one for losses and the other for gains, named in the chart’s notes, and the total sits apart above the bars in words. Set the names flush left at the drawing’s edge.

text: Bars from one zero line let the eye compare every gain and loss by length (Rule 14.4), and the side of the line tells the direction before a reader reaches a figure. A figure set across zero from its bar lines up with every other figure, so the column reads as a list. Color repeats what position says, so the chart still reads in grayscale (Rule 14.5).

rules.builders: Form diverging-bar: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s25; encode.include keeps small items in the table and out of the drawing.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which items gained and which lost between two dates, and how much each moved.

use_instead.when: Every item moved the same way and the reader wants them ranked
The reader follows a gain or loss election by election
Where each item started and ended matters as much as the change

correct.caption: Which federal agencies gained or lost civilian employees?

rules.title: Show who held the advantage in each term as arrows from one center line.
rule: Use a diverging bar with arrows to follow an advantage that can change sides, such as a House majority, one election or term at a time. Give each term one row in time order, with an arrow from a center line toward the side that held the advantage, as long as the advantage, and the figure at its tip. Draw every arrow in one neutral ink, name each side over its half, and print the party’s name on the first row and wherever the advantage changed sides (Rule 14.7).

text: An arrow’s direction answers who held the advantage and its length answers by how much, so a reader running down the rows sees both the size of each lead and every change of control. One ink for every arrow keeps color from taking a side (Rule 14.7); position and the printed names carry it.

rules.builders: Form diverging-bar-arrows: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s26; encode the two sides’ counts as left and right, and the form draws their difference.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how big a lead was in each election or term, and when it passed from one side to the other.

use_instead.when: One change per item between two dates, ranked by size
Many items gained or lost over one window, with no sequence of terms
The seats in one chamber at one time, each seat counted

correct.caption: How large was the House majority’s lead in seats in each Congress?

rules.title: Mark the moments that explain a line on the line itself.
rule: Use a line with event notes for one series and the events a reader needs to read it. Draw the subject series as a heavy line on a scale that starts at zero unless the change is the point (Rule 14.4), any comparison series thin and gray, each series named on its line, and short notes inside the plot with leaders to the points they explain. Break the line where the publisher changed its method, and never draw across the break (Rule 14.11).

text: A note set at the point it explains lets the reader see the event and the change together, without a legend to match. The note says what happened and when, and leaves the cause to the evidence (Rule 13.2), so the timing of a rise is never offered as proof of what caused it.

rules.builders: Form line-event-notes: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s02; annotations place each note, and encode.break marks a method change.
rules.use_when: The reader asks what happened to one measure and when, and a few dated events explain its turns.

use_instead.when: One group should be read against several others
The series has a period with no figure
An amount a law sets changes on dates

correct.caption: What happened to child poverty when the expanded child tax credit was paid, and after it lapsed?

rules.title: Give each group its own panel, lit against the others in gray.
rule: Use a multi-line with one highlighted when several groups share a measure and the reader compares each with the rest. Give each group one small panel on one shared scale, with the group’s own line heavy in ink over the others in thin gray, and its name and latest value over the panel. Past four groups the panels carry the comparison (Rule 14.8).

text: Four lines on one plot tangle where they cross, and a key makes the reader match colors. A panel per group, with the others drawn gray in every panel, keeps each line readable and puts every gap in view, and one scale keeps the panels honest with each other.

rules.builders: Form multi-line-highlight: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s05; labels.panels sets each panel’s group and order.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how far apart groups stand on one measure, and whether the gaps have closed.

use_instead.when: Dozens of series, with one the story follows
The groups differ in size and the question is growth
One series with the events behind it

correct.caption: How far apart are homeownership rates by race, and has the gap closed?

rules.title: Draw every series thin and gray, and light the one the story follows.
rule: Use a line field when dozens of series share one scale and the story follows one of them: draw every series as a thin gray line, so the reader sees the spread, and draw the subject in ink on top with its name and latest value at its end. Where two series tie for the title’s point, draw both in ink. Set the national series apart as a dashed line in the text’s ink with its own end label, name one or two gray lines at the field’s edges where it helps, and carry every series in the table.

text: Colored lines for 50 states tangle into noise, and the same lines in gray read as one shape: the range every place moved within. One line in ink against that shape shows where the subject sits without a key, and the table gives every other series a reader may want to find (Rule 14.8).

rules.builders: Form line-field: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s27; labels.lit names the series in ink (a list for a tie), labels.apart the dashed national line and labels.named the gray lines named at the field’s edges.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how one place or group moved against all the others, and the whole field matters as context.

use_instead.when: Four series or fewer, each one the reader follows
The series differ greatly in size and the reader compares growth from one date
Each series needs reading on its own

correct.caption: How did home prices move in every state, and where did they rise most?

rules.title: Draw noisy monthly counts as columns, with an average line through them.
rule: Use columns with a moving average for a monthly count that swings from month to month. Draw each month as a column from zero and the average as a heavy line over them, hatch the preliminary months and dash the average where it includes one, and label the latest month with its status. Where the publisher gives a margin of error, say in a note which months pass it.

text: Each column shows one month as the survey counted it, and the average shows where the months are heading, so a single bad month reads as a dip in a trend that holds. A survey’s monthly figure carries error, and the note that says which drops pass the margin keeps a small swing from reading as news (Rule 14.9).

rules.builders: Form columns-moving-average: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s14; encode.status marks preliminary months.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how many jobs the economy added or lost each month, and the trend matters more than any one month.

use_instead.when: A rate or a level that moves smoothly
The same count across many industries or places
A month has no figure at all

correct.caption: How many jobs did the economy add each month?

rules.title: Set a word-sized line inside a sentence to show a trend’s shape.
rule: Use a sparkline, a line as tall as the type and a few words wide, where a sentence or a table row names a trend. Print the first and last figures in the words beside it, put a dot on the last value, scale each line to its own lowest and highest values, and leave out axes and gridlines.

text: A sparkline gives the shape of a series in the space of a word, so the reader keeps reading. Each line takes its own scale, so its height says nothing about size, and the figures in the sentence carry the amounts.

rules.builders: Form sparkline: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s28; each sentence in labels.sentences holds {spark} where the line sits and takes its figures from the data.
rules.use_when: The reader is reading a sentence or scanning a row and needs the shape of a trend next to its figures, without leaving the line.

use_instead.when: The reader needs to read values off the line, or to compare lines on one scale
The same trend runs down many rows of a table
Many parts of one total need one shared scale

correct.caption: Has the number of civic and social organizations grown or shrunk?

rules.title: Show one trend across many parts as small area panels on one scale.
rule: Use small-multiple area sparklines when the same measure runs across many parts of a whole. Give each part one small panel on one shared vertical scale, with the area from zero under the part’s line, the whole’s line in gray in every panel, and the change printed over the panel. Order the panels by the change the title names, and set the totals above them.

text: One shared scale lets a reader compare panels at a glance, and the gray line of the whole in every panel shows which parts ran ahead of it. Small panels give each part room that one plot of many lines cannot.

rules.builders: Form area-sparklines: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s13; labels.panels sets the order and labels.context the gray line in every panel.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which parts of a total grew and which shrank over the same span.

use_instead.when: The reader looks the parts up row by row, with their figures
The parts differ greatly in size and the question is growth since one date
One total, where its size is the point

correct.caption: Which sectors added jobs since January 2022, and which lost them?

rules.title: Fill the space under one total when its size is the point.
rule: Use an area chart for one total over time, such as the people an industry employs: fill from zero up to the line, run the line along the top of the fill and set the scale from zero. Draw one series, and name what the fill counts inside it.

text: A filled area asks the eye to judge size, so it fits a count of people, dollars or places. Under a rate, the same fill shows a size the numbers never had. The scale starts at zero for the reason a bar does (Rule 14.4): a fill cut off above zero makes a small fall look like a collapse.

rules.builders: Form area: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s29, or copy specs/s29.json and point it at a new dataset.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how big a total is and how far it has grown or shrunk, and the amount itself carries the story.

use_instead.when: The values are a rate or a share, where a fill would show an amount the figures do not hold
Several groups make up the total and the reader needs each one
The counts swing month to month and the trend needs an average
The same total runs across many industries or places

correct.caption: How many people work for newspaper publishers?

rules.title: Draw an amount a law fixes between dates as a step line.
rule: Use a step line for an amount a law or rule holds until the next change, such as a tax credit per child. Keep the line flat through each period, move it straight up or down in the period the change takes effect, and print each level’s amount on it. Name the law that made each change beside its step or in the notes.

text: A line that slopes from one date to the next tells the reader the amount crept up over the years, when the law moved it all at once. Flat runs and straight risers show what each tax year carried, and the law named at each riser tells the reader who made the change.

rules.builders: Form step-line: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s30, with x the year or date each amount takes effect and y the amount.
rules.use_when: The reader asks what a rule set at each date, and the value stays fixed between one change and the next.

use_instead.when: Survey figures that move between dates, such as a rate
The reader needs the dates each part of one law takes effect more than an amount
The dates of events matter and no amount changes

correct.caption: How has the law changed the child tax credit’s top amount per child since 2017?

rules.title: Stop the line at a missing month and name the gap where it falls.
rule: When a series has no value for a period, end the line before it and start it again after it, shade the missing period and name it on the chart. The table keeps the row and prints Not published in its cell.

text: A line drawn across a missing month invents a figure the publisher never printed, and the reader cannot tell it from the measured months around it. A named gap shows where the record stops, and the table says the same in words (Rule 14.11).

rules.builders: Form line-data-gap: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s31; leave the missing period’s cell empty in the data file and give the gap its words in labels.gap.
rules.use_when: The reader follows a monthly or yearly series with a period the publisher left blank, such as a month a survey did not run.

use_instead.when: The method changed and the publisher prints two estimates for the year it changed
No month is missing, and the latest months are preliminary, marked as Rule 14.11 sets

correct.caption: What was the unemployment rate each month, and which month is missing?

rules.title: Set dated events on lanes along one true scale of time.
rule: Use a timeline for dated events that fall into a few threads: one lane per thread, each event placed at its date on one scale that keeps true spacing, with its date and name printed, and shaded bands for stretches the notes explain. On a phone each lane becomes a dated list under its thread’s name.

text: True spacing shows the reader that some decades held many changes and others few, which an evenly spaced list hides. Lanes sort events by kind without a key, and a phone list keeps every date and name readable where a lane would crowd (Rule 14.12).

rules.builders: Form timeline: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s09; labels.lanes names each thread and its question.
rules.use_when: The reader asks what happened when, and which kind of change each event was.

use_instead.when: When each part of one law takes effect
Each event or period carries a count
A measure moves between the events

correct.caption: Which rule changes since 1870 decided who counts, who governs, who owns and who checks?

rules.title: Show when each part of a law starts as a bar from its date.
rule: Use an implementation timeline when a law or rule starts in parts: one row per part in date order, with its date, section and a plain line on what starts, over a lane where a bar begins on the start date and runs on. Hatch the first year of a part that reaches each plan or program as its own year begins, mark a deadline with a dot, and mark the day the President signed the law on every lane.

text: A President signs a law on one day, and its parts start on many, and a reader who hears it passed may expect the change at once. One lane per part, each starting on its own date, shows the wait for each part, and the hatched year keeps a plan-year date from reading as one day for everyone.

rules.builders: Form implementation-timeline: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s32; labels.kinds maps each row’s kind to approved, deadline, phase or start.
rules.use_when: The reader asks when a law they have heard about will touch them, and its parts start on different dates.

use_instead.when: Dated events from many sources, with no parts of one law
An amount the law changes from period to period
Where one bill stands on its way to becoming law

correct.caption: When does each part of the 2026 law on pharmacy benefit managers take effect?

rules.title: Index many series to one start when the reader compares growth.
rule: Use an indexed line when the reader compares series of far different sizes by how fast they grew: divide each by its own value at one base date and multiply by 100, so every line starts at 100. Draw the line at 100 thin in the secondary ink, so it reads apart from the series, and name the base over the value axis. Give one series the ink and the rest gray when there are more than four (Rule 14.8), and name every line at its end with its latest index, the figure always on the line of its name. Under 600 px, name the inked lines in a key inside the plot and list the others under it with their latest index, highest first.

text: On a scale of dollars, a $35 billion source that quintuples lies flat beside a $3 trillion one. An index puts every series at 100 on the same date, so a line’s height shows growth alone. A fast-growing source can stay small, so the notes give each highlighted series’ amount and share, and the reader does not take a fast-growing small source for a large one.

rules.builders: Form indexed-line: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s33; labels.base names the date that equals 100, the form computes each index from the raw values, and labels.list_title heads the list under a narrow plot.
rules.use_when: The reader asks which of several measures grew fastest since a date, and their sizes are too far apart to share a scale in their own units.

use_instead.when: The reader needs the amounts themselves, or how big each part is
Each series needs its own panel to be read closely
Only one series matters and its moments need explaining

correct.caption: Which sources of federal revenue grew fastest since fiscal 2016?

rules.title: Size each period’s circle by its count along one line of time.
rule: Use a bubble timeline when each period or event carries one count and the reader looks for when the counts swelled: one circle per period along one line, its area in proportion to the count (Rule 14.4), with a key of round sizes above. Give every circle a light fill and an outline, mark a period with nothing to count with a tick, and dash the outline of a period still under way. Where neighbors would merge, set them alternately above and below the line, each touching it, and sum a long run of small counts in one sentence.

text: A circle sized by area lets a reader see a count grow from a handful to hundreds without a scale that crushes the small years. The eye judges area loosely, so the key gives round sizes, the notes give the largest figure, and the table gives every one.

rules.builders: Form bubble-timeline: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s34; encode.complete false dashes a period still under way, and labels.phone_from sums the periods before it in words and staggers the rest.
rules.use_when: The reader asks when something became common across a long span, and the exact count for each period matters less than the change in scale.

use_instead.when: The reader needs to compare counts closely, period by period
The events matter for what they were, and no count goes with them
One continuous measure over time, such as a rate

correct.caption: How often has the Senate voted on ending debate, Congress by Congress?

rules.title: Show what a household keeps as its earnings rise, cliffs and all.
rule: Use a benefit-cliff line to show what one household has after taxes and benefits at each level of earnings. Draw the household’s resources as a heavy line, its earnings alone as a dashed diagonal, and a light band from any drop to the earnings where the household is back where it was. Name the drop in words with its size, and state the household and the rules the chart assumes. Built on invented rules, the chart carries “Illustrative data” beside its top edge (Rule 13.8).

text: A raise that leaves a family with less is hard to believe until the reader sees the line fall. The diagonal of earnings alone shows what the benefits add, and the band shows how far the family must climb to get back, so the size of the trap reads before any figure. Real cliffs depend on the state, the family and the year, so the chart names the household it assumes.

rules.builders: Form benefit-cliff: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s35; the form finds the largest drop and the climb back from the rows.
rules.use_when: The reader asks whether earning more leaves a family better off, and benefits that end at set earnings may say no.

use_instead.when: An amount the law sets for each year, with no earnings involved
How one benefit’s value has changed over time

correct.caption: What does one family keep as its earnings rise and benefits phase out?

rules.title: Use a run chart to watch a process against its own median.
rule: Use a run chart, a reference form, for a measure an office tracks week by week, such as days to answer a request. Draw the values as dots joined by a line, a dashed line at their median, and a shaded run where six or more points in a row sit on one side of it. Oath & Action draws one when a story follows how a public service performs over time.

text: Every process wobbles, and a single high week proves nothing. A run of points on one side of the median is a simple, standard sign that something changed, which keeps a reader from taking noise for news or missing a real shift.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw a run chart from line-event-notes or line-data-gap with the median added as a note, until a story needs its own form.
rules.use_when: The reader asks whether a process has changed or is only wobbling, and the measure has no outside target to compare with.

use_instead.when: The measure is a public agency’s count or survey and its moments need explaining
The reader compares one value with a target or a range
The values swing month to month and a moving average shows the trend

correct.caption: A weekly measure of a process as a line of dots around a dashed median line, with a shaded stretch where six weeks in a row sit above the median, a run long enough to signal a shift in the process.
correct.label: Run chart, a sketch

rules.title: Lay each year over the same months to show a season’s pattern.
rule: Use a cycle or seasonal chart, a reference form, when a measure repeats each year: months along the bottom, one thin gray line for each earlier year, and this year in ink, ending at its latest month. Name this year and the earlier years on the lines.

text: A measure that rises every winter looks like a crisis on a plain line each December. Laying the years over the same months shows the season as the shape every year shares, and puts this year’s difference from that shape in view.

rules.builders: No kit form: draw it from line-field, with the month as x and each year as a series, until a story needs its own form.
rules.use_when: The reader asks whether this month is high or low for the time of year, as with claims that rise every winter.

use_instead.when: The publisher removes the seasonal swing, and the trend is the question
Many years of one measure, with one the story follows
Monthly counts with an average through them

correct.caption: Months from January to December along the bottom, one thin gray line for each earlier year and a heavy line for this year so far, so a reader compares each month with the same month in other years.
correct.label: Cycle or seasonal chart, a sketch

rules.title: Avoid streamgraphs, whose layers float on a baseline no one can read.
rule: Leave streamgraphs out of every Oath & Action piece. Show parts of a total over time as small multiples, one panel per part on one scale, or as a stacked area with a flat baseline when the total matters.

text: A streamgraph stacks its layers around a wavy center line, so no layer sits on a flat baseline and a reader can measure none of them against a scale. When one layer swells, every layer above and below it bends, and a reader takes that bend for a change in layers that never moved.

rules.builders: No kit form, by design; draw the parts with area-sparklines (s13) or, from round 2, the stacked area form.
rules.sketch_alt: A streamgraph beside small multiples of the same illustrative data: the middle part holds steady, and its band bends in the streamgraph and lies flat in the small multiples.
rules.use_when: Never: a reader who asks how the parts of a total changed over time gets a truer answer from small multiples or a stacked area.

use_instead.when: Each part’s own trend matters
The total and its parts both matter, with a few parts
The reader reads one part against the rest

correct.caption: A streamgraph beside small multiples of the same illustrative data: the middle part holds steady, and its band bends in the streamgraph and lies flat in the small multiples.
correct.label: Streamgraph, a form that misleads

rules.title: Use a 100 percent bar to compare how wholes of different sizes divide into the same parts.
rule: Draw each whole as one bar of the same length, split into its parts in a fixed order, with the part the question is about first from the left and in the subject ink. Step the other parts toward the page color, hatch the last, and print the first part’s share with the whole’s count at the right of each bar. Sort the bars by that share, and draw a dashed line across them in the text’s ink, with its own label, where an overall share helps the reader place each one (Rule 14.6).

text: Every bar runs the same length, so the eye compares shares as lengths from one shared left edge. The first part is the only one that starts on that edge, which is why it takes the question’s part and the ink. Printing the share and the count keeps a small whole from looking as solid as a large one.

rules.builders: Form percent-bar: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s10, or copy specs/s10.json and point it at a new dataset; labels.parts sets each part’s fill and words, labels.share the words at the right, and labels.mark_at the line across the bars.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how the mix of parts compares across several wholes, such as how much of each answer rests on documented fact, and the wholes differ in size.

use_instead.when: Each whole splits two ways and the question is which part is larger
The parts’ sizes matter more than their shares
The reader should see each item as one mark to count
The mix changes across years

correct.caption: How much of each everyday answer rests on documented fact?

rules.title: Use a stacked share bar with a midline when the question is which of two parts is the larger.
rule: Split each bar into its two parts as shares of the whole, the part the question asks about from the left and the other in the track gray, with a 1 px line in the text’s ink at half. Sort the bars by the first part’s share, print it at the right of each bar, and set a national or total row first, apart from the rest. The row the title names takes the red point while its red stays within 5 percent of the drawing at every width (Rule 05.1), or the subject ink where Rule 14.6 sets ink in its place, as for a state, and every other first part takes light gray.

text: The midline turns a question about majorities into a question of which side of one line a bar ends on. A shared left edge keeps the first part a length from zero, and the second part in pale gray keeps every bar whole without competing with the share that answers the question.

rules.builders: Form stacked-share-bar: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s43; encode.left and encode.right name the two share columns, labels.apart sets a total row first, and labels.named or labels.point names the row the title names.
rules.use_when: The reader asks where one of two groups is the majority, such as the states where renters outnumber owners, and the answer turns on which side of half each bar ends.

use_instead.when: Each whole splits into three or four parts
The two parts are counts whose sizes the reader compares
The reader needs the margin of error around each share

correct.caption: In which states do renters make up the larger share of households?

rules.title: Use a waterfall to show how steps add up to a total or a gap.
rule: Read the steps from top to bottom: each one floats from the running total before it to the one after, a step that adds in diverging pair B’s green and a step that takes away in its dark blue, with every value printed beside its bar with its sign. A total runs from the zero line in the context gray and starts the count again; the result the title names takes the subject ink, never red (Rule 14.6). A thin line joins each step to the next. Keep every line the publisher prints, or fold small lines within one side only and list each in the table.

text: A waterfall keeps the running total in view, so the reader sees where the result comes from as well as how big it is. Floating bars still read as lengths, because each one measures its own step on the shared scale, and the printed signs let a reader who sees no color still tell the two directions apart.

rules.builders: Form waterfall: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s44; encode.kind marks each line, labels.totals the kinds drawn from zero, labels.named the result the title names, and labels.names the printed names.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how a set of additions and subtractions arrive at a result, such as how a year’s receipts and outlays add up to the deficit.

use_instead.when: The parts make one whole with nothing taken away
The reader compares the parts’ sizes alone
The same steps are compared across years

correct.caption: How did fiscal 2026’s receipts and outlays add up to the deficit?

rules.title: Use a unit chart when each mark stands for one thing a reader can count.
rule: Draw one square for each item, grouped by year or kind and placed by the category the question asks about, such as toward voters above a line and away from voters below it. Give each category its own style that holds in gray print (solid, open, gray, hatched or dashed), name each one in a key, and print the count for every group.

text: A square for each item lets a reader count, so a total never has to be taken on trust. Styles that differ in fill and outline keep the categories apart in gray print and for a reader who sees no color.

rules.builders: Form unit-chart: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s08; labels.categories sets each category’s style and words, labels.mirror the two categories set above and below the line.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how many things of each kind there are, the items are few enough to draw one by one, and seeing each item makes the count concrete.

use_instead.when: The items run to the thousands
The reader compares shares of wholes of different sizes
The reader asks about seats in a chamber

correct.caption: Have the rules been moving toward voters or away from them?

rules.title: Use stacked columns for a total over time that splits into a few parts.
rule: Stack up to four parts in each column in one fixed order, the largest or the base part on the zero line, in the categorical inks in their order: Charcoal, Verdigris, Prussian, then Stone, always hatched (Rule 14.5). Leave a 1 px gap of the page color between parts, name each part beside the last column, or in a key on a phone, and print the total over the columns the title or notes discuss. Keep a part too thin to see at its true height, and say so in a note.

text: Columns from one zero line show the total as a height a reader can compare year to year. Only the first part sits on that line, so the parts above it are read best by their share of the column, which is why the order never changes and the part the story follows goes first or last.

rules.builders: Form stacked-column: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s45; encode.parts lists the columns in stacking order, encode.total the published total, and labels.totals_at the columns whose totals print.
rules.use_when: The reader asks how a total changed over a run of years and what it was made of, such as how many homes were finished each year and in what kind of building.

use_instead.when: There are more than four parts
The parts’ shares matter more than the total
One year’s parts are the question
The total alone tells the story

correct.caption: What kinds of homes were finished each year?

rules.title: Use a stacked area of shares to follow a whole’s mix over many years.
rule: Stack up to four parts as shares of each year’s total, from 0 to 100 percent, in the categorical inks in their order with Stone hatched (Rule 14.5). Name each band inside it at its right end and print its last share past the edge. Say in a note when a part starts or stops, such as a program that began partway through the window.

text: Shares that add to 100 every year let a reader see one part grow at another’s expense across decades. Only the baseline and the line at 100 are straight, so the bands between them are read by their thickness, which is why each one is named where it ends and its last share is printed.

rules.builders: Form stacked-area: node work/build/chart-kit/oa-chart.mjs build s46; encode.parts lists the columns from the bottom, and labels.offset draws shares (expand) or amounts (zero).
